title: Svayamprabha asks nothing
hookLine: cover your eyes, you're out, and she asks nothing back
carry: sattvic dana: a gift that asks nothing back

cards: Fed and rested, the monkeys tell Svayamprabha everything: Rama, Sita, Ravana, the search, Sugriva's deadline. She listens. And then Hanuman asks the question that's been sitting under all that good food.
How do we get out? They came in by holding each other in the dark, through a long, twisting passage. It's not easy to leave this place alive, Svayamprabha tells them.
Not without help. Then she says she'll help.

teach.h: CLOSE YOUR EYES. OUT BY THE SEA.
teach.b: Svayamprabha says she'll bring them out by the power of her austerities. Close your eyes, she says. Cover them with your hands.

They do. And in an instant they're outside, standing near the shore, with the great southern ocean roaring in front of them. She shows them where they are, wishes them well, and goes back into her cave.
Then the cruel part. Inside the cave it didn't feel long.

teach.h: THE MONTH IS GONE. SHE ASKS NOTHING.
teach.b: But outside the trees are in flower, and when Angada counts the days, the month Sugriva gave them is gone, and they still have nothing to report. Now look at what Svayamprabha asks in return. Nothing.

In a book full of bargains, a pact for a pact, an army for a kingdom, she gives food, rest and rescue, and walks back into the dark. Hindus have a word for giving: dana. And the Bhagavad Gita sorts gifts by kind.

teach.h: SATTVIC DANA: A GIFT THAT ASKS NOTHING BACK.
teach.b: The highest, the sattvic gift, the pure one, is given simply because it ought to be given, at the right time and place, to someone who can do nothing for you in return. Svayamprabha's gift fits exactly.
The monkeys can't repay her, and she doesn't ask.

That's why many Hindu families give quietly: a donation with no name on it, food sent to the temple kitchen, what Hindi speakers call gupt daan, secret giving. The giving is the point, not the thanks.
And now, on the shore, with the sea in front of them and the deadline behind them, the southern party has a new problem.

how: Many Hindu families give dana quietly, without their names. Some later tellings, such as the Adhyatma Ramayana, have Svayamprabha go on to meet Rama; in Valmiki she simply goes back into her cave.

o: a sea goddess who guards the southern shore
the ascetic who leads the monkeys out of her cave
a spirit who traps travelers in a dark cave

games.q: leaving the cave — tap the pairs.
p: a gift to one who can't repay
a sign the month has passed

s: the Gita calls a gift pure when it goes to someone who can't repay it
that's the sattvic gift, given simply because it ought to be given.
they come out with the month already gone
the deadline has passed and they have no news.
she asks nothing, and goes back into her cave.

games.q: you're Svayamprabha. the monkeys are safe by the sea. they have nothing to pay you with. what do you do?
o: ask them to bring you treasure from Lanka.
wish them well and go back into your cave.
make them promise to tell Rama your name.
games.why: she goes back into her cave asking nothing: the gift the Gita calls sattvic, pure.

practice: Close your eyes, or cover them gently with your palms, the way the monkeys did. Breathe in and remember a time someone helped you and asked nothing back.

Breathe out and choose one small gift you can give today with no name on it: a donation, a meal, a favor nobody will hear about. If you pray, offer it quietly to God; if you don't, just let it go out without waiting for thanks.

wordCard.voice: Svayamprabha, who leads the monkeys out of her cave by her own power. Eyes covered, and they're out by the southern sea, but the month is already gone.

orig.note: Sanskrit ṛkṣabila: 'bear's hole', Valmiki's name for the cave, from ṛkṣa (bear) + bila (hole, cave).

carryVoice: Your line: sattvic dana, a gift that asks nothing back. Svayamprabha walked back into her cave. That's day five hundred ninety-seven.
